synopsis: PIRT ranks the physical phenomena that matter most and provides the graded basis for allocating validation evidence in NRC EMDAP: highly ranked phenomena require test data, while lower-ranked phenomena receive reduced emphasis [f14640, f8089, f7836, f14646]. The assessment base uses separate-effects tests, integral-effects tests and scaling analysis to isolate phenomena, exercise coupled behavior and establish applicability of test-rig data [f14644]. For collision-mitigation validation, the assessor package should rank brake fade, dust attenuation, glare and mount vibration, trace scenarios to hazards and EMESRT/ISO 21815, and use the ranking to determine which physical tests to retain [f8030, f14651]. Within the validated parameter hull, changes not touching ranked phenomena can be documented and evaluated through simulation alone, whereas changes touching them should trigger brake calibration and sensor field-of-view and detection checks at the new mount [f7912, f7913]. Full machine-family re-validation is recommended only for variants outside that hull or introducing a new PIRT phenomenon, such as a new sensor type or articulated steering; this is identified as expert opinion [f7918]. The method's subjectivity remains an explicit concern: a peer-reviewed criticism calls for treating it explicitly, and experts disagree about accepting subjective rankings without that treatment [f14652, f8194].

relations.note: Both require evidence for highly ranked phenomena and reduced emphasis for low-ranked phenomena.
